question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2022, behavioral ecologist Marisol Dunweather claimed that carrion crows living in dense city districts solve a novel puzzle feeder faster than rural carrion crows do, because city crows are more at ease around unfamiliar objects.
• A team led by Corwin Aldessa at the Ferrowmere Bird Lab tested 30 crows from dense city districts and 30 crows from rural farmland on a puzzle feeder: a clear box with a sliding lid that had to be pushed aside to reach a peanut.
• The city crows opened the lid in an average of 74 seconds; the rural crows opened it in an average of 131 seconds.
• The team also gave each of these 60 crows its familiar feeding dish, filled with food, and placed a brightly colored plastic cone beside the dish.
• The team recorded the number of seconds from the moment the cone was set down until the crow first took food from the dish.
• The crows took food after an average of 38 seconds for the city group and 38 seconds for the rural group.
• Each crow was tested alone, once per test, at the same time of day and after food had been withheld for the same period, and every test was recorded on video from a blind about 15 meters away.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Dunweather's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Dunweather's claim: the city crows and the rural crows took food from the familiar dish after the same average time, 38 seconds, once the cone was placed beside it.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Dunweather's observation but not their explanation: the city crows opened the puzzle feeder in an average of 74 seconds to the rural crows' 131 seconds, yet both groups took food from the familiar dish after the same average time, 38 seconds, once the cone was placed beside it.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Dunweather's claim: the city crows opened the puzzle feeder in an average of 74 seconds, compared with an average of 131 seconds for the rural crows.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Dunweather's claim and show the two groups were otherwise comparable: the city crows opened the puzzle feeder in an average of 74 seconds to the rural crows' 131 seconds, and both groups took food from the familiar dish after the same average time, 38 seconds.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it matches each part of Dunweather's claim to the data that bears on it. Dunweather's sentence says two things: that city crows solve a novel puzzle feeder faster than rural crows do, and that this happens because city crows are more at ease around unfamiliar objects. The puzzle-feeder test bears on the first part. The city crows opened the lid in an average of 74 seconds, compared with 131 seconds for the rural crows, so the faster solving Dunweather described did appear. The dish test bears on the second part. A crow that is more at ease around an unfamiliar object should go on feeding from its usual dish sooner when a brightly colored cone is placed beside it, so the time before first taking food shows whether the city crows really are more at ease. The city crows and the rural crows both took food after an average of 38 seconds, so there was no sign that the city crows were more at ease. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The note about testing each crow alone under the same feeding schedule and filming from a blind describes the method and does not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical dish-test times (38 seconds for both groups) do count against Dunweather's explanation about being at ease around unfamiliar objects, but the claim also says that city crows solve the puzzle feeder faster, and the feeder results (74 versus 131 seconds) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 74 versus 131 seconds do fit the first part of Dunweather's claim, that city crows solve the puzzle feeder faster, but the claim also says this happens because city crows are more at ease around unfamiliar objects, and the dish-test results (38 seconds for both groups) show no such difference. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the dish-test result as a check on whether the groups were comparable rather than as a test of the explanation. In the dish test, an unfamiliar object (the brightly colored cone) was set beside a crow's familiar dish, and the team timed how long the crow waited before taking food, so the test bears on how the crows responded to an unfamiliar object, the very thing Dunweather's 'because' clause is about. The identical times (38 seconds) therefore show that the two groups did not differ in that response, which fails to support the explanation instead of confirming it. Nothing in the notes presents the dish test as a check that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2022, pollination biologist Ilsabet Orrowin claimed that honeybees that feed on nectar containing a low dose of caffeine return to that kind of flower more often than bees fed plain nectar do, because caffeine helps the bees remember the flower's scent.
• A team led by Kasimir Dovrenko at the Marlowe Fen Research Station released 40 bees fed caffeinated nectar and 40 bees fed plain nectar into a flight cage containing two kinds of flowers.
• Over three days, the bees fed caffeinated nectar made an average of 52 return visits per bee to the kind of flower they had fed on; the bees fed plain nectar made an average of 31.
• The team also tested bees from the same colony: it fed 60 bees caffeinated nectar and 60 bees plain nectar, and then trained all 120 bees by pairing a floral odor with a drop of sugar solution.
• Twenty-four hours later, the team puffed the odor alone, with no sugar, at each bee and recorded whether the bee extended its tongue (proboscis).
• The tongue was extended by 60% of the bees fed caffeinated nectar and by 60% of the bees fed plain nectar.
• The flight cage measured 4 meters by 3 meters, and the odor puffs in the laboratory test lasted 4 seconds each.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Orrowin's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings bear out Orrowin's claim: the bees fed caffeinated nectar made an average of 52 return visits per bee to the kind of flower they had fed on, compared with an average of 31 for the bees fed plain nectar.
answer_b: The team's findings undermine Orrowin's claim: 60% of the bees fed caffeinated nectar and 60% of the bees fed plain nectar extended their tongue when the odor was puffed alone 24 hours after training.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Orrowin's observation but not their explanation: the bees fed caffeinated nectar made an average of 52 return visits per bee to 31 for the bees fed plain nectar, yet 60% of the bees in each group extended their tongue when the odor was puffed alone 24 hours after training.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Orrowin's claim and show the two groups were otherwise comparable: the bees fed caffeinated nectar made an average of 52 return visits per bee to 31 for the bees fed plain nectar, and 60% of the bees in each group extended their tongue to the odor alone.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it matches each part of Orrowin's claim to the data that bears on it. Orrowin's sentence says two things: that bees fed low-dose caffeinated nectar return to that kind of flower more often than bees fed plain nectar, and that this happens because caffeine helps the bees remember the flower's scent. The flight cage counts bear on the first part. The bees fed caffeinated nectar made an average of 52 return visits per bee, compared with 31 for the bees fed plain nectar, so the greater number of return visits Orrowin described did appear. The odor test bears on the second part. After the odor had been paired with sugar, puffing the odor alone and recording whether a bee extended its tongue shows whether the bee still responds to that scent a day later, which is what the 'because' clause is about. Tongue extension was recorded for 60% of the bees fed caffeinated nectar and 60% of the bees fed plain nectar, so there was no sign that caffeine strengthened the response to the scent. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the size of the flight cage and the length of the odor puffs describe the method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 52 versus 31 return visits per bee do fit the first part of Orrowin's claim, that bees fed caffeinated nectar return more often, but Orrowin also said this happens because caffeine helps the bees remember the flower's scent, and the odor test (60% tongue extension in both groups) shows no stronger response to the scent in the caffeine group. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical tongue-extension percentages (60% in both groups) do count against Orrowin's explanation about the scent, but the claim also says that bees fed caffeinated nectar return to that kind of flower more often, and the flight cage counts (52 versus 31 return visits per bee) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the odor test as a check on the groups rather than as a test of the explanation. The notes describe the odor test as a record of whether each bee extended its tongue to the scent alone 24 hours after the scent had been paired with sugar, which bears on Orrowin's 'because' clause about the scent. The identical percentages (60% in both groups) therefore fail to support the explanation instead of confirming the claim. Nothing in the notes presents the test as a check that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the explanation as added support for the claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2023, education researcher Imrey Palloway claimed that high school students given a 20-minute early-afternoon nap score higher on a late-afternoon geometry quiz than students who instead read quietly, because the nap makes students less drowsy in the late afternoon.
• A team led by Dorian Halsworth at Oakhollow Academy assigned 40 students to a 20-minute nap and 40 students to 20 minutes of quiet reading, each in the early afternoon.
• At 4:00 p.m., all 80 students took the same 25-question geometry quiz. The nap group averaged 19.4 correct answers; the reading group averaged 14.2 correct answers.
• Just before the quiz, each student also completed a 10-minute task, widely used to gauge how alert a person is, in which a dot appeared on a screen at random intervals and the student pressed a button as soon as it appeared.
• The team recorded, for each student, the number of responses that took longer than half a second.
• The nap group averaged 6.3 such slow responses per student; the reading group averaged 6.3 such slow responses per student.
• Quiz papers were scored by teachers who did not know which students had napped, and the screen task was run on identical laptops in a single classroom.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Palloway's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings bear out Palloway's claim and show the two groups were otherwise comparable: the nap group averaged 19.4 correct answers on the quiz to the reading group's 14.2, and both groups averaged the same number of slow responses on the screen task, 6.3 per student.
answer_b: The team's findings undermine Palloway's claim: the nap group and the reading group averaged the same number of slow responses on the screen task, 6.3 per student.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Palloway's claim: the nap group averaged 19.4 correct answers on the geometry quiz, compared with an average of 14.2 correct answers for the reading group.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Palloway's observation but not their explanation: the nap group averaged 19.4 correct answers on the quiz to the reading group's 14.2, yet both groups averaged the same number of slow responses on the screen task, 6.3 per student.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it matches each part of Palloway's claim to the data that bears on it. Palloway's sentence says two things: that students given a 20-minute early-afternoon nap score higher on a late-afternoon geometry quiz than students who read quietly, and that this happens because the nap makes students less drowsy in the late afternoon. The quiz results bear on the first part. The nap group averaged 19.4 correct answers and the reading group averaged 14.2, so the higher scores Palloway described did appear. The screen task bears on the second part. The notes describe this task as a gauge of how alert a person is, and a student who is less drowsy is more alert and should have fewer responses that take longer than half a second, so the number of slow responses shows whether the napping students were less drowsy shortly before the quiz. Both groups averaged 6.3 slow responses per student, so there was no sign that the nap group was less drowsy. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about who scored the quiz papers and the laptops and classroom used for the screen task describe the method and do not bear on either part of the claim.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it misreads the screen task result as a control rather than as a test of the explanation. The notes describe the screen task as a gauge of how alert a person is, recorded as how often each student's response took longer than half a second, which bears on Palloway's 'because' clause about the nap's effect on students just before the quiz. The identical averages (6.3 slow responses per student) therefore show no difference between the groups on the measure relevant to the explanation, which fails to support it rather than confirming it. Nothing in the notes presents the screen task as a check that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical numbers of slow responses (6.3 per student for both groups) do count against Palloway's explanation about the nap reducing drowsiness, but the claim also says that napping students score higher on the quiz, and the quiz results (19.4 versus 14.2 correct answers) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The quiz averages of 19.4 versus 14.2 correct answers do fit the first part of Palloway's claim, that napping students score higher, but Palloway also said this happens because the nap makes students less drowsy, and the screen task results (6.3 slow responses per student in both groups) show no such difference. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2022, cognitive psychologist Rhea Fenwraith claimed that adults who brainstorm while hearing recorded café chatter at moderate volume list more unusual uses for everyday objects than adults who brainstorm in silence do, because the moderate noise makes people more physiologically aroused, or keyed up.
• A team led by Anders Hallisey at Brindlemoor University had 40 adults brainstorm for 10 minutes while café chatter played at moderate volume and 40 other adults brainstorm for 10 minutes in silence, listing uses for a brick, a paper clip, and a bucket.
• Judges who did not know which condition each person was in counted the uses they rated original. The café group averaged 14.6 original uses per person, and the silence group averaged 9.8.
• During the task, the team also recorded the electrical conductance of each participant's skin through sensors attached to two fingertips, in microsiemens; skin conducts electricity more readily when its sweat glands are more active, as they are when a person is keyed up.
• The average skin conductance was 6.2 microsiemens for the café group and 6.2 microsiemens for the silence group.
• Participants were tested one at a time in a sound-treated booth, and the café recording was played through headphones.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Fenwraith's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings bear out Fenwraith's observation but not their explanation: the café group averaged 14.6 original uses per person to the silence group's 9.8, yet both groups showed the same average skin conductance, 6.2 microsiemens.
answer_b: The team's findings undermine Fenwraith's claim: the café group and the silence group showed the same average skin conductance, 6.2 microsiemens, during the brainstorming task.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Fenwraith's claim: the café group averaged 14.6 original uses per person, compared with an average of 9.8 original uses per person for the silence group.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Fenwraith's claim and show the two groups were otherwise comparable: the café group averaged 14.6 original uses per person to the silence group's 9.8, and both groups showed the same average skin conductance, 6.2 microsiemens.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it matches each part of Fenwraith's claim to the data that bears on it. Fenwraith's sentence says two things: that adults who brainstorm while hearing café chatter at moderate volume list more unusual uses than adults who brainstorm in silence, and that this happens because the noise makes people more physiologically aroused. The judges' counts bear on the first part. The café group averaged 14.6 original uses per person, compared with 9.8 for the silence group, so the advantage Fenwraith described did appear. The skin conductance recordings bear on the second part. According to the notes, skin conducts electricity more readily when its sweat glands are more active, as they are when a person is keyed up, so the fingertip readings show whether the noise made participants more keyed up during the task. Both groups averaged 6.2 microsiemens, so there was no sign that the café chatter made people more physiologically aroused. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The note about the sound-treated booth and the headphones describes how the sessions were run and does not bear on either part.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical skin conductance averages (6.2 microsiemens for both groups) do count against Fenwraith's explanation about physiological arousal, but the claim also says that people brainstorming amid café chatter list more unusual uses, and the judges' counts (14.6 versus 9.8 original uses) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 14.6 versus 9.8 original uses do fit the first part of Fenwraith's claim, that the café group lists more unusual uses, but Fenwraith also said this happens because the noise makes people more physiologically aroused, and the skin conductance recordings (6.2 microsiemens for both groups) show no such difference. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the skin conductance result as a control rather than as a test of the explanation. The notes link skin conductance to sweat-gland activity of the kind that occurs when a person is keyed up, which is exactly what Fenwraith's 'because' clause is about. The identical averages (6.2 microsiemens) therefore show that the café chatter did not change this measure, which fails to support the explanation instead of confirming it. Nothing in the notes presents the recordings as a check that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the claim.
